new_statements.quote: MSL compounds adhere to what has been observed for compound forms in previous signed language research. For example, compounds are smooth; they are similar in duration to other non-compound signs; the second unit of the compound is stressed, and in the articulation of a compound there is some reduction of the individual signs it is comprised of.
new_statements.citation: Yoel, Judith. 2009. Canada's Maritime Sign Language. PhD dissertation, University of Manitoba. Section 7.2.3 'The Impact of Language Contact on Compound Signs', p. 245.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (331 pp, Canon scan with text layer, no PDF metadata). PDF page 260 = printed p. 245, section 7.2.3 'The Impact of Language Contact on Compound Signs'. new_statements.rule_in_words: In MSL compound signs (MSL^MSL, BSL^MSL and hybrid MSL^ASL compounds such as BOY^FRIEND), prominence ('stress') falls on the second, i.e. final, unit of the compound; the first unit is reduced (shortened, hold lost, cf. p. 120). This is a sign-language notion of stress (movement/duration prominence), and the author frames it as MSL conforming to what is known for compounds in other signed languages rather than as an independent phonological analysis. No statement exists about prominence within simplex (non-compound) signs.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Footnote 55 (p. 120, Bencie Woll p.c.) notes only that in BSL the second unit of a compound is not the semantic head except in fingerspelled compounds; p. 120 also notes that in BSL the first component of a compound is often shortened or loses its hold, and that one component may be dropped (TEACHER).
new_statements.domain_note: Compound signs only (two-sign lexical compounds observed in narrative and elicited data); not a word-stress rule for the lexicon at large and not phrase-level prosody. Sign language: 'stress' here is visual-manual prominence, not pitch/intensity. Confidence is low because the statement is one sentence in a sociolinguistic dissertation without measurements or minimal pairs.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Maritime Sign Language (MSL, mari1381, ISO nsr) as used by elderly Deaf signers in Nova Scotia (Halifax and small towns), the BSL-descended variety, contrasted with ASL; hybrid MSL/ASL compounds are included in the compound observation. No dialect subdivision is named. Sign language: the 'stress' statement concerns manual prominence in compounds, not spoken word stress; reviewers may judge it out of scope for a word-stress catalog.

sources.quote: MSL compounds adhere to what has been observed for compound forms in previous signed language research. For example, compounds are smooth; they are similar in duration to other non-compound signs; the second unit of the compound is stressed, and in the articulation of a compound there is some reduction of the individual signs it is comprised of.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic/lexicostatistic study (Swadesh and Parkhurst lists vs ASL and BSL, narratives, identity), not a grammar; no phonology chapter. The only stress statement is in section 7.2.3 (p. 245) on compound signs: 'the second unit of the compound is stressed, and in the articulation of a compound there is some reduction of the individual signs'. Footnote 55 (p. 120, Bencie Woll p.c.) concerns compound headedness in BSL, not stress. Nothing on prominence in simplex signs.
History and sociolinguistic status only; no phonology or prosody. Cites Yoel 2009 (MSpace handle 1993/21581), Ethnologue, Carbin & Smith, CBC 2019.
